title: How Ben 10 Made Me Fall in Love with Watches
excerpt: A childhood obsession with the Omnitrix somehow turned into a full-blown love for watches — and it never really went away.
content: I love watches. Probably more than I love some people. There's something about strapping a tiny piece of time to your wrist that makes life feel a little less meaningless — and it all started with Ben 10 and his Omnitrix, the coolest piece of alien tech to ever grace a cartoon.

content.text: The Omnitrix is not a weapon, it's a responsibility. It's more than just a watch. It's the key to an entire universe.

content: As a kid I wasn't just watching Ben 10, I was living it — toy Omnitrixes, knockoff Omnitrixes, even paper ones when the budget got tight. I'd slap it on, tap it like Ben, scream "HUMUNGOUSAUR!!!", and proceed to wreck the living room like a five-year-old on a sugar high. Turns out my only real power was destroying furniture and getting yelled at.

Eventually I traded plastic alien watches for real ones — not because I grew up, just because society insisted. The Omnitrix was fiction, but the obsession was very real, and it's stuck around as an appreciation for design, mechanics, and the aesthetic of a well-crafted timepiece. A good watch makes you feel like you've got your life together, even when you're really just staring at it wondering where your time — and money — went.
Ben 10 made me fall in love with watches, and that love never left. I can't turn into aliens anymore, tragically, but I can still rock a sick watch and pretend I've got it all figured out.

title: Not All Heroes Wear Capes (But They Do Carry Heavy Backpacks)
excerpt: Superhero Syndrome, bullies, and the exhausting weight of feeling like you have to protect everyone.
content: Okay, real talk, I've got what people call Superhero Syndrome (aka the Superman Complex). Basically, I'm that person who feels like I need to save everyone, fix everything, and make sure nothing bad happens to my people. Like, if something's coming their way, it better go through me first. Sounds like main character energy, right? Well… it's actually lowkey exhausting.

I think it comes from my parents. They're literally built different. They'll help people even if they hate them, and they always drop this one line: "Agar hum bhi unke jaise ban jaye to unme aur hum me kya farq rahega" (If we become like them, then what's the difference between us and them?). That one line pretty much tattooed itself on my brain. And boom, now I can't just stand by when something wrong is happening.

Back in school, I used to mess with bullies just to protect other kids. One time I even went against my own friends because they were teasing a girl. At that moment, I didn't care about losing them, I cared about doing the right thing. The twist? That girl's been one of my closest friends for the past 5 years. We still talk a lot. That one choice literally rewrote my story.

content.text: The Dark Side of Playing Hero 🖤

content: Here's the stuff no one tells you: being a "hero" is heavy.

Whenever something bad happens to my people, I instantly blame myself. If someone says something mean to my friend, my brain goes: "If I was there, I would've protected her. It's all my fault." Even when it's not. Then I end up hating myself, cursing myself, and ruining my day.

content.text: If I can't save the one small girl in front of me, how can I become a hero who saves everyone?

content: If you feel the same, remember this: you don't have to take every hit to prove your worth. Protecting people also means protecting your own peace. Even heroes need to log off and recharge.
Sometimes the bravest thing to say is: "I can't fix everything, but I'll stand with you anyway." 🤍

title: Fear of Ageing is Really a Fear of the Unknown – And Modern Society is Making It Worse
excerpt: On turning 19, watching everyone younger seem to have it figured out, and why that fear isn't really about age at all.
content: Some nights I lie in bed, phone clutched to my chest, staring at the ceiling thinking — "Am I already late?" I'm 19. Still young. Still figuring it out. But somehow, it feels like life is sprinting ahead and I'm jogging in flip-flops.

Every time I open Instagram, I see a 14-year-old launching a startup, a 15-year-old going viral with some insane edit or song, or a 13-year-old coding apps while I'm over here trying to decide what to eat for dinner. Like, bro, I was still learning how to solve linear equations at that age. Why does everyone look like they've figured it all out?

This isn't just about ageing. It's about uncertainty. It's about the fear of not knowing what's next — and that fear has been romanticized, monetized, and constantly thrown at our faces through reels, stories, and #grindset posts. It's not about wrinkles. It's about whether I'll ever make it. Whether I'll be enough.
And when you're constantly seeing people younger than you winning, you start feeling like you're losing — even if you're not. It's toxic. It's not even a race anymore, it's a panic attack with WiFi.

Ageing in this context isn't about turning older. It's about drifting further from the version of yourself you thought you'd be by now. It's about watching timelines blur while people scream "you've got time" but also "start young or stay broke." Like okay?? Pick a struggle??

And I'm not saying success is bad. Not even jealous (well, maybe a little). I'm just tired of pretending I'm not confused. That I've got some secret blueprint. Because I don't. Most of us don't. And that should be okay.

I've started to think that maybe the only cure to this fear is acceptance — that the unknown will always exist. You can't out-plan it. Can't out-hustle it. But you can choose how you show up in the middle of all the noise.

content.text: Power comes in response to a need, not a desire. You have to create that need.

content: Ageing isn't scary when you stop measuring life by viral moments and start measuring it by real ones. Like laughing until you cry. Like sharing a moment with someone who gets you. Like writing this blog post and realizing… I'm not behind.
I'm just on my own timeline.
And if you're reading this, maybe you are too.
